title: A robot starts at the top-left of an m by n grid and may move only right or down. Count how many distinct paths reach the bottom-right.
shortTitle: Unique Paths: count grid paths moving right or down
keyPoints: Define dp[i][j] as the number of distinct paths from the top-left to cell (i, j).
The first row and first column are all 1 because along an edge there is exactly one straight path.
The recurrence is dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] since the robot arrives from above or from the left.
Space reduces from O(m*n) to O(n) using a single rolling row updated left to right.
A closed-form combinatorial answer exists: C(m+n-2, m-1), choosing which moves are down among all moves.
Time is O(m*n) for the DP approach and O(m+n) for the combinatorial formula.

s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i][j] = paths from above + paths from the left; edges are all 1.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Unique Paths** – a grid DP problem where `dp[i][j]` counts the number of distinct paths from the top-left to cell `(i, j)` when only rightward and downward moves are allowed.
- **Base cases** – the entire first row and first column are all 1, because along an edge there is exactly one straight path.
- **Recurrence** – `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]`, summing paths from above and from the left.
- **Space optimisation** – a single rolling row of size n, updated left to right, replaces the full grid.
- **Closed form** – the binomial coefficient C(m+n-2, m-1) gives the answer in O(m+n) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a sealed document must be routed across a grid of branch offices, moving only east or south. The number of distinct routes to any office is the sum of routes to the office to its west and the office to its north.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths is a grid dynamic programming problem. I define dp[i][j] as the number of distinct paths from the top-left to cell (i, j), given that the robot moves only right or down. The base cases are the entire first row and first column, all ones, because along an edge there is exactly one straight path.

For every interior cell, the robot arrives from directly above or directly from the left, so the number of paths is the sum of the paths to those two neighbors. The answer is the bottom-right cell. I reduce memory to a single rolling row because each row depends only on the one above it, and there is also a closed-form combinatorial answer as C(m+n-2, m-1).

Edge cases include 1x1, 1xN, and Mx1 grids (all have exactly one path), and very large grids where the combinatorial formula risks overflow. The DP grid is equivalent to Pascal's Triangle, where each cell is a binomial coefficient.

At the National Bank of India, I modeled a loan approval workflow as a grid where a request moved to the next approval stage or across to the next department. The single-row DP counted the distinct approval routes from intake to final sign-off efficiently.

Remember one sentence: paths to a cell equal paths from above plus paths from the left, with edges all one.
